prize_parts.citation: for the detection of a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with the IceCube observatory, opening neutrino astronomy

statement.case_for: The discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos is what I mean by letting nature supply the clues. A purpose-built instrument, a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice, found a flux that nobody could have derived from theory, and it has since been confirmed through several independent analysis channels (through-going muons, contained cascades, starting events). It opens a new observational window, speaks to the century-old question of where cosmic rays come from, and has already produced a first source association (TXS 0506+056) and the NGC 1068 and Galactic-plane results. It has an existential flavour too: we are listening to the most violent accelerators in the universe with a particle that crosses it unhindered. The credited pair, Halzen as the conceiver and driving force of the cubic-kilometre concept and Karle as a leader of construction and the discovery analyses, is compact enough to fit within the three-person limit without strain.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. A collaboration of hundreds, the AMANDA precursor, and the competing deep-water efforts (Baikal, ANTARES, now KM3NeT) mean that two names will inevitably be contested, and our supplied text does not settle whether Karle or another IceCube leader or analysis lead has the stronger claim to the decisive step. Second, the source identification rests so far mostly on one experiment, and the origin of the bulk of the diffuse flux is open. If the committee judges that the discovery is the diffuse flux, I think that is sufficient. If it wants the source picture to be settled first, then the prize is premature by some years, and the lattice-clock candidate (B045) is the safer, broader-supported alternative.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first for the same reason I do, as detector-driven discovery with careful background rejection, but notes that the source identifications are less independently confirmed by KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD and doubts whether two names fairly split the hardware and analysis contributions.
responses.response: I agree with the distinction and want to keep it sharp. The prize case is the diffuse flux, which was seen in several independent channels within the same detector with different techniques, and which does not depend on TXS 0506+056 being the final word on sources. On attribution I only half agree that the hardware-versus-analysis split is a weakness. Halzen's conception and Karle's role across construction and analysis cut across that split, which is a reason for the pair rather than against it. But I accept that independent confirmation from a second observatory would make the case easier, and I would like the committee to check the historical record for AMANDA-era leaders before we commit.

responses.point: Kroll puts the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock first as a measurement breakthrough with 1e-18 uncertainty, relativistic geodesy and a path to redefining the second, noting independent reproduction in many national labs.
responses.response: This is the candidate I find hardest to argue against, and the breadth of support it has (five of eight members rank it) deserves respect rather than a dismissal. My reservation is about the nature of the discovery. The clock is a superb achievement of precision and control, but the headline is an accuracy figure and an enabling tool; what we have learned about nature from it is still prospective, while the neutrino flux told us something we did not know. I am also wary, as you are, of how much is new relative to the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize. I would not block B045, and I list it as my first alternative, but I would want the redefinition of the second, or a clear fundamental-physics result, to carry more weight in the citation.

responses.point: Mehlig places topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect first as a clean, general mechanism that has reshaped how phases are classified, noting that the supplied credit omits Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and that recognition is overdue.
responses.response: I find the conceptual argument persuasive, and it is the case that most resembles my own taste for results that survive disorder and generalise. But the attribution problem you raise is, in my view, more serious than the opening ballots made it sound. If the HgTe proposal belongs to Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, with one of them deceased, and Hasan's three-dimensional work is a separate stage, then a three-name prize either mis-credits or splits the story. Mele's omission in Olsson's version and Hasan's omission in yours are both costly. Until the committee can state who made the decisive step, I cannot rank B040 above a case with a clear chain of credit, though I would rank it above the quantum-technology candidates.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as a clean case of a calculation predicting a striking behaviour that experiment then realised, creating the field of moire quantum materials, while noting the open priority questions about earlier theory.
responses.response: I put B038 seventh and I would like to explain why rather than only state it. The prediction-then-observation narrative is attractive, and I accept that many groups have reproduced the correlated phases. But the mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved and the twisted-material field is still moving fast, so we would be recognising a platform before we know what it has taught us. Our own 2011 theory has the further complication of earlier flat-band work by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto that you mention. I am willing to be moved if you can argue that the correlated insulator is the lasting discovery regardless of how the pairing question resolves, but I think a few more years would make the choice easier and the credit cleaner.

uncertainties: Whether Halzen and Karle are the two people with the strongest claim to the decisive contribution, given the AMANDA predecessor, other IceCube leaders and the competing deep-water programmes.
Whether the committee regards the diffuse flux alone as sufficient, or wants the source identification (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) independently confirmed by another observatory first.
How much weight the broad but second-place support for the lattice clock (B045) should carry against a smaller group of first-place votes for IceCube.
Whether a quantum-technology prize (B026, B007, B028) is better delayed after the 2025 superconducting-circuits prize.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. My connections (David Gross as PhD supervisor, Thomas Van Riet as co-author, the Uppsala string-theory group) do not touch any of the credited names, and I am a theorist outside neutrino astronomy and AMO physics, so I rely on colleagues for experimental credit details.
